fullText:
Benford’s Law: https://t.co/XK8wbZbhTW

Fraud detection is just one of its many practical powerful applications!

Amazon Summary:

“This book provides the first comprehensive treatment of Benford's law, the surprising logarithmic distribution of significant digits discovered in the late nineteenth century. Establishing the mathematical and statistical principles that underpin this intriguing phenomenon, the text combines up-to-date theoretical results with overviews of the law’s colorful history, rapidly growing body of empirical evidence, and wide range of applications.

An Introduction to Benford’s Law begins with basic facts about significant digits, Benford functions, sequences, and random variables, including tools from the theory of uniform distribution. After introducing the scale-, base-, and sum-invariance characterizations of the law, the book develops the significant-digit properties of both deterministic and stochastic processes, such as iterations of functions, powers of matrices, differential equations, and products, powers, and mixtures of random variables. Two concluding chapters survey the finitely additive theory and the flourishing applications of Benford’s law.

Carefully selected diagrams, tables, and close to 150 examples illuminate the main concepts throughout. The text includes many open problems, in addition to dozens of new basic theorems and all the main references. A distinguishing feature is the emphasis on the surprising ubiquity and robustness of the significant-digit law. This text can serve as both a primary reference and a basis for seminars and courses.”

fullText:
Pretty cool that we clearly have an emerging form factor for what AI might look like for the foreseeable future as autonomous systems dedicated to specific tasks or domains.

This is a huge leap past the LLM wrapper days because the new expectation is that you can finally farm out more sophisticated work to the agent to tackle for you. And you can reliably trust that work can get accomplished properly (still with a human in the loop) because of far better tool and computer use, and the general intelligence of the models improving. 

1) The tool and computer use capability increases in the models mean that you can provide the agent with far more granular access to external data systems and other software to operate. This means, in effect, the agent begins to execute workflows similar to how a person would have in that same function. And where there isn’t existing software, the agent just builds it itself. This is a huge unlock. 

2) Next, the actual capability of the models are improving in just about every vertical domain. The models can make far better judgment calls in legal, do deeper bio research, scan for security issues in code, understand supply chain processes, and more. Obviously in many of these spaces then models still have worse intuition than people, but that will only get better.

3) Finally, the harnesses and surrounding infra — sandboxes, file systems, data pipelines, etc. — allows for longer running agents, agents to be able to work on arbitrarily complex or long tasks, process data at enormous scale, and more. Few of these components worked well for AI even a year ago, but we now have many of the core primitives necessary for more autonomous systems.

When combined with the right UX, implementation, and change management for the human oversight and coordination, it’s clear that these autonomous systems will become quite powerful in a wide variety of enterprise workflows. 

We’re starting to see them in IT automation, cyber operations, drug discovery, manufacturing, AI research, and more spaces. You can almost imagine one or more of these systems for every role in the economy. Quite a bit of opportunity ahead.

fullText:
I sought the right course
to teach students without force.
The subject was applied math,
to be approached with ease and no wrath.

This was no simple token
since earlier courses were broken,
and the legacy pedagogy
can't you see, was a bit dodgy.

So I didn't stand up and say "Let Us
Start Learning Some Calculus!"
I knew better than try that,
to avoid resistance and a spat.

Instead I left out the name,
seriously, who can blame?
And so namelessly I taught it.
In the end, they totally bought it.

Life with Calculus!
Math Lovers-Я-us.
🩷❤️🧡💛🤍💚🩵💙💜🤎🖤

- Original "poetry" by @KirkDBorne 

The true backstory: Among the various undergraduate and graduate courses that I taught at the University (GMU) was an introductory computational & data sciences course. Many of the students in the first day of class expressed strongly their fear of math and their hope that the course was only low-level math. I told them not to worry—I would teach them whatever math they needed to know. So, I taught them calculus (integral and differential) but I didn’t tell them it was calculus until after their first quiz and homework assignments involving calculus. When I finally told them that they had just learned calculus, they were stunned. Some had tears in their eyes. Some thanked me profusely saying it was best course they ever had and they wanted to learn more math. In fact, the one young man who was most adamant against math on the first day of class, by the end of the semester, was the most profoundly changed and grateful student that I ever taught. I still remember his handshake after the final exam and the excitement in his voice looking forward to taking more math courses—to make up for all that he missed previously due to misinformed fear. (This is a true story, not AI slop.)

From the Back Cover:

"This textbook explains the fundamentals of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) without assuming advanced knowledge of mathematics and programming. MCMC is a powerful technique that can be used to integrate complicated functions or to handle complicated probability distributions. MCMC is frequently used in diverse fields where statistical methods are important – e.g. Bayesian statistics, quantum physics, machine learning, computer science, computational biology, and mathematical economics. This book aims to equip readers with a sound understanding of MCMC and enable them to write simulation codes by themselves."

"The content consists of six chapters. Following Chapter 2, which introduces readers to the Monte Carlo algorithm and highlights the advantages of MCMC, Chapter 3 presents the general aspects of MCMC. Chapter 4 illustrates the essence of MCMC through the simple example of the Metropolis algorithm. In turn, Chapter 5 explains the HMC algorithm, Gibbs sampling algorithm and Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, discussing their pros, cons and pitfalls. Lastly, Chapter 6 presents several applications of MCMC. Including a wealth of examples and exercises with solutions, as well as sample codes and further math topics in the Appendix, this book offers a valuable asset for students and beginners in various fields."
